blindSummary:
This state/province is the origin and continuing custodian of the country's student human-rights protections: the model ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was "first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for this state/province", was adopted by the capital's education office in 2012, and spread to other offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave. When the capital's council - controlled by the governing national party, acting on a campaign begun by religious groups and parents' coalitions in August 2022 - abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, this state/province stood among only six of the country's sub-national education offices still enforcing such ordinances, and a teacher here was quoted warning that abolishing the ordinance outright "will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector".

School non-discrimination rules concern residents and students. No enforcement action, event, incident, or police practice favouring or disfavavouring a visible trans visitor is documented for this state/province, and no repeal move against its own ordinance is on record. (An earlier version of this record credited this state/province with blocking the capital's 2024 abolition; that challenge - the sit-in protest and the July 2024 supreme-court petition that suspended the abolition - belongs to the capital's education office. What remains is the origin-and-continued-enforcement record, whose traveler-facing impact is minimal.)
blindSourceSummaries: A national daily's report (28 April 2024) on the capital council's abolition of the student human-rights ordinance twelve years after the capital office adopted it: the ordinance model was "first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for this state/province"; abolition was pushed by the governing national party's council majority after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six sub-national education offices - this state/province's among them - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the capital's superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led national legislature said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A teacher based in this state/province defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.
blindLocalsOnly: The protections credited to this state/province - the 2010-origin student rights ordinance it continues to enforce - bear on enrolled students and school staff, not on visitors.
